rv.q: It’s a scene that captures what makes this new “Tristan” the event of the season at the Met.
The answer, of course, is all of the above.
Mr. Sharon’s direction wove together the different strands of the opera and the production, exploring the narrative and themes while encompassing the humanity of the characters.
Davidsen’s titanic voice is made for Isolde, and indeed the wild fury of her Act I narrative and curse pins the audience to the back of its seats.
The Met’s latest production, under the direction of Yuval Sharon, is stronger on the philosophical than the psychological.
In this case it achieves just the opposite.
The impact of evening was stunning.
Have you ever witnessed both a Tristan and an Isolde physically plausible and vocally up to everything that Wagner throws at them, from violent cursing to heartbreaking tenderness?
Problematic as the production is, this Tristan is one for the ages — see it if you can, or at least listen to the March 21 matinee performance, which also will be shown live in HD in movie theaters.

For the moment, we have his "Tristan und Isolde," which as he writes in his book, "might appear to be single-handedly responsible for deforestation" but also engages "new ideas, new sounds, new visions" that "create conditions for people to think differently."
The registered effects are both gratuitous and superfluous, a director showing he has ideas but still doesn’t quite understand what opera is all about.

It would be believable that Sharon had the intent of creating an experience that transcends the tale’s ancient origins, but he ultimately positions the story neither here nor there, yet still tangibly gets in the way of the music.

The debuting 47-year-old American has given the Met a bafflingly awkward Tristan that not only failed to impress, but also let down the company’s superb musical forces, especially Lise Davidsen and Michael Spyres as its astonishing title pair.

cn.t: Davidsen and Spyres earn rapturous praise as vocally ideal leads in the Met's new "Tristan," though Sharon's conceptually bold production divides critics—some find it philosophically rich, others consider it distracting.
